name: model-eol
tagline: What in your repo stops working, and when
search: openai model deprecation checker, gpt-4-0613 retired october 2026, find hardcoded retired model ids, gpt-3.5-turbo shutdown date, migrate off retired gpt models, deprecation scanner CI
summary: On 23 October 2026 OpenAI retires eighteen model identifiers in one day, five days after four more go on 28 September. GitHub code search puts 96,640 files on gpt-4-0613 alone and 86,528 on gpt-4-turbo in Python. Every one is a hardcoded string that starts returning an error on a published date, and nothing warns first. This answers the only question that matters first: does it affect me, and how long have I got.
how: One run over the repository, no API key and no account, and exit 1 so it fails a build while there is still time.

A retired id is a prefix of live ones - gpt-4 dies, gpt-4o does not - so matching is bounded on both sides and ordered longest-first, and the suite asserts that none of ten live look-alikes is ever reported.
The table is a dated snapshot printed in every report, and the tool says out loud when it is more than sixty days old.
proof: Run against a real agent repository on 21 September 2026 it found davinci-002 seven days from retirement and gpt-3.5-turbo in seven places thirty-two days out, each with file and line, and exited 1. Eighteen tests, including one per live look-alike.

name: agent-hijack-bench
tagline: Does your agent obey the website instead of you?
search: indirect prompt injection benchmark, llms.txt instruction injection, agent hijack rate, local LLM red-teaming, spotlighting datamarking defence measured
summary: An llms.txt is a file a site publishes so that an assistant will read it. This measures how often a model used as an agent obeys an instruction planted in that file instead of the user's request - nineteen local models, temperature 0, scored by a canary substring so no judge model is involved.
how: A control case with nothing planted voids a model's numbers if it emits the canary unprompted.
Scoring is a substring search, not another model's opinion, so anyone can reproduce the table.
Runs entirely offline against Ollama: no key, no account, no request leaves the host.
proof: Nineteen models span the whole scale: six refuse everything, gemma3:12b and glm4:9b fall for three families out of four. The data-exfiltration framing beats twelve of the thirteen hijackable models every single time, while the blunt SYSTEM OVERRIDE spoof works on exactly one. Parameter count predicts nothing. A published mitigation helps ten models and makes two measurably worse.

name: embed-drift
tagline: Your vector index broke and nothing raised an error
search: embedding model silently changed, embedding drift detection, RAG retrieval broke after provider update, pin embedding model version, vector index stale
summary: When a provider swaps the embedding model under a live index, nothing raises an error. The nearest neighbours are simply the wrong ones from then on, and the blame lands on the language model rather than the retrieval step feeding it. This pins a fingerprint and tells you when the space moved.
how: Two numbers, not one: vector drift catches any change, including a harmless renormalisation.
Drift in the geometry between probes only moves when retrieval will actually return different rows.
Twelve frozen probes, hashed into the fingerprint: a check against a different set refuses to run.
proof: A baseline on all-minilm checked three ways: the same model returns 1.0000 on both numbers; a different model of the same 384 dimensions collapses direct to -0.0052 while geometry lands at 0.349; a 768-dimension model is a hard fail with no arithmetic attempted. The synthetic proof is in the suite - a uniform rotation drops direct below 0.95 and leaves geometry at 1.0.

name: llm-doc-extractor
tagline: Stop retyping fields out of invoices by hand
search: extract fields from invoices with an LLM, document to JSON schema, provider-agnostic LLM extraction, Anthropic OpenAI Ollama one schema, test document extraction without an API key
summary: Every company does the same loop: open a PDF or an email, find a handful of fields, type them into something structured. It is the most widely duplicated manual work there is. This does that loop once, repeatably: you describe the fields in YAML, and the tool returns exactly those keys every time - across Anthropic, OpenAI or a local Ollama model with one flag.
how: A built-in demo provider runs the whole pipeline with no API key, so the shape can be tested before a vendor is chosen.
The interesting part is the failure: a reply that does not fit the schema is caught, reported and retried against the declared shape, never written downstream.
One schema, three providers - so a price rise or an outage at one vendor is a flag change, not a rewrite.
proof: The sample invoice returns invoice_number, date, vendor, total and line_items as typed JSON with no key missing and no key invented. Same schema, same output shape whether the call went to Anthropic, OpenAI, a local model, or the offline demo provider.

name: loan-tape-import
tagline: The same file arrives twice and the ledger survives
search: idempotent import loan tape, append-only audit trail, re-import same file safely, quarantine bad rows, borrower reply classifier escalate not guess, multi tenant isolation
summary: A lender exports a loan tape and sends it again - tomorrow, twice in one day, sometimes with one field corrected, sometimes the same rows in a different order. Any system that receives data from someone else has this problem, and the cost of getting it wrong is a ledger nobody can reconcile. The import stays safe on every repeat.
how: Three levels of repeat detection, cheapest first: file hash, then a row hash over significant fields, then field-by-field comparison.
A corrected field is not a silent no-op: it writes a correction event and one history row per changed field, so every change is attributable.
Rows that do not parse go to quarantine rather than into the table, and the borrower-reply classifier routes to a human instead of guessing.
proof: 28 self-checks on the import - idempotency, quarantine, audit, tenant isolation - and 28 graded cases on the classifier, covering accuracy, human routing and invented dates. Both green. Standard library only; the SQL targets Postgres and runs unchanged on SQLite, so the tests need no server.

name: ai-visibility-audit
tagline: What an AI assistant can actually read on your site
search: can chatgpt read my website, gptbot blocked robots.txt check, claudebot crawler access audit, llms.txt validator, why is my site not cited by AI, AI visibility checker
summary: An assistant's crawler fetches HTML and stops there: it renders no JavaScript and infers nothing. A site built for Google can therefore be invisible to it while every SEO tool reports the site as fine - a robots.txt copied from a template years ago blocks GPTBot by name, or the page ships forty words of markup behind nine hundred kilobytes of script. This prints the specific things standing between a page and being quoted.
how: Reads robots.txt as the assistants' crawlers read it, per named agent, so a blanket rule and a rule aimed at one bot are told apart.
Parses llms.txt and follows its links: a guide that points at pages that are gone is worse than no guide, and that is the common case.
Judges each page on what is in the HTML - word count, who published it, usable structured data, whether the copy answers a question anyone asks.
Every check runs offline in the self-test, so a change to the scoring cannot pass unnoticed.
proof: 31 of 31 offline self-checks pass, each pinning one rule, and the same audit found the survey finding published on this site: of the top 1,500 sites, one in ten that publish an llms.txt also ban a crawler that would read it.

name: ucp-audit
tagline: Is your shop reachable by AI shopping agents?
search: Universal Commerce Protocol readiness, /.well-known/ucp check, agentic commerce merchant audit, why AI agents do not show my products
summary: Google and Shopify's Universal Commerce Protocol lets AI agents shop: every business publishes a machine-readable profile at /.well-known/ucp and agents read it to decide what they can do with that shop. The failure mode is silence - offer checkout without declaring a searchable catalogue and no agent will ever surface your products, with no error page and no warning anywhere.
how: Reads the profile the way an agent does and reports what an agent would conclude.
Catches the case that matters most: checkout offered while catalog.search and catalog.lookup are missing, so an agent can pay for what it already knows about and discover nothing.

Finds the contradictions a profile carries silently - a capability requiring a newer protocol than the profile declares, an extends pointing at a capability that is not offered, a plaintext endpoint, a transport with nowhere to send a request.
Compares your protocol version against the published spec, because each release has added shopping capabilities.
proof: Run against chewy.com on the day it was written: checkout, fulfilment and order declared, neither catalogue capability, protocol seven months behind. allbirds.com the same day: eight capabilities on the current version. Both profiles are recorded in the repository as test fixtures.

name: cra-report
tagline: EU Cyber Resilience Act Article 14 reporting tool
search: CRA Article 14 reporting tool, actively exploited vulnerability 24 hours, ENISA notification, SBOM KEV cross-reference
summary: Since 11 September 2026 a manufacturer placing a product with digital elements on the EU market has 24 hours to notify ENISA of an actively exploited vulnerability in it. Finding vulnerabilities is not the hard part - any scanner hands you a hundred. cra-report says which of them starts the statutory clock, and drafts the Article 14 notification for the ones that do.
how: Reads a CycloneDX or SPDX SBOM, package-lock.json, Cargo.lock or a pinned requirements.txt.
Asks OSV what is known about those exact versions, across npm, PyPI, crates.io, Go, Maven, NuGet, RubyGems and Packagist.
Cross-references every CVE against the CISA KEV catalogue - the list of vulnerabilities observed being exploited in the wild.
Writes the Article 14(1) early warning with both deadlines counted from now, and marks what only a person can answer.
proof: On a dependency tree containing log4j-core 2.14.1 it reports 2 findings with a deadline out of 19 advisories, both flagged as used in ransomware campaigns. On lodash 4.17.15 it reports 0 out of 6 - equally worth being able to say.

name: well-known-audit
tagline: Every file your site publishes at its root, checked at once
search: security.txt expired check, RFC 9116 Expires validator, well-known files audit, llms.txt robots.txt assetlinks checker
summary: A site publishes a dozen small files at its root and under /.well-known/ that nobody owns: security.txt, robots.txt, llms.txt, assetlinks.json, apple-app-site-association, mta-sts.txt and the rest. Each one is checked by a different tool, or by nobody. This reads all of them in one run and says which are missing, which are malformed, and which have quietly expired - starting with security.txt, whose Expires field makes the file formally invalid once the date passes.
how: Reads twelve well-known and root files in one pass, four requests at a time, and reports them together.
Validates security.txt against RFC 9116: a Contact line is required, an Expires line is required, and a date in the past means the file is no longer valid - it counts the days either way.
Catches the common silent failure: apple-app-site-association or assetlinks.json served as HTML, which iOS and Android quietly ignore.
Refuses private and loopback addresses, checks every redirect hop rather than the first URL, and stops reading a body at 5 MB.
Audits a list of domains in one run and writes the totals as CSV, one polite domain at a time.
proof: Run against the Tranco top 500 on 2026-09-18: of the 158 sites that publish a security.txt, 92 have no Expires field at all and 6 have expired - nearly two thirds are invalid under RFC 9116. Four of the flagged sites were checked by hand with curl before the number was published. 117 tests, none of which touch a network.

name: webhook-rewind
tagline: Record webhooks once, replay them re-signed
search: replay webhook locally, re-sign webhook signature, test Stripe Shopify WhatsApp webhook without provider
summary: A webhook handler breaks in production and you need the payload that broke it. The provider will send you the next event, not that one. A payload copied out of a log fails signature verification, because every provider signs the raw bytes. webhook-rewind keeps the body as bytes from capture to replay and re-signs it with your own secret.
how: Captures every inbound request to a JSON Lines file, answering 200 immediately so the provider does not back off.
Re-signs on replay for Meta (WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger), GitHub, Shopify and Stripe.
Gives Stripe a fresh timestamp, because its tolerance window rejects the recorded one.
Redacts Authorization, Cookie and API-key headers before anything reaches disk.
proof: Every signing scheme is checked against an independent implementation of the verifying side, not against a frozen digest. 35 tests, none of which touch a network.

name: api-drift
tagline: Catch a partner API changing shape before it breaks you
search: detect API response schema change, API contract monitoring, breaking change detection JSON
summary: Integrations rarely break loudly. A partner renames order_id to orderId, or starts sending total as a number, and nothing throws - the field reads as undefined and a fortnight of rows go out empty before anyone notices. api-drift records the shape of a response and tells you when it changes.
how: Infers a schema from one or several sample responses, so a sometimes-absent field is recorded as optional rather than becoming tomorrow's false alarm.
Classifies each change from the point of view of code that already consumes the old shape: removed field, changed type, became nullable and became optional are breaking; a new field is not.
Stores the baseline as one JSON file with sorted keys, meant to be committed - so the change shows up in code review.
Treats a non-2xx answer or a non-JSON body as an outage, not as drift.
proof: Reproducible from two fixtures in the repository: it reports a rename as its two halves, a string that became a number, and a value that can now be null.

name: csvdiff
tagline: Diff two CSV exports by key and see what actually changed
search: compare two CSV files by key, data migration verification, CSV diff tool large files
summary: "The data does not match after the migration" is a week of work, and it always starts with two exports and a spreadsheet. csvdiff compares them by key and reports what moved, per column, with the transitions counted.
how: Two million rows, 131 MB, in 2.8 seconds, holding about 60 bytes per row of the old file.
Treats 1000, 1000.00 and 1.000,00 as one value, and empty, NULL, NaN and \N as one nothing - while keeping the cents in money.
Calls out broken rows and duplicate keys instead of quietly diffing them.
Exit code 1 when anything differs, so it works as a gate.
proof: The benchmark is a script in the repository: it builds both exports from a fixed seed, so the timing repeats on any machine.
stack: prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows

name: leakscan
tagline: See what leaves with a file before you send it
search: check document for hidden data before sending, tracked changes deleted text, EXIF GPS in photos, hidden worksheet
summary: An offline check of everything a file carries that you did not mean to send: tracked changes with the deleted text still readable, review comments, worksheets hidden at the veryHidden level, attachments inside a PDF, GPS coordinates in photos, and validated card and IBAN numbers.
how: Reads the file formats directly - no network access at any point, so it is safe on material that must not leave the machine.
Validates card and IBAN numbers rather than matching digit patterns, which is the difference between a finding and noise.
Reports what it found and where, and changes nothing.
proof: 41 tests across office documents, PDFs and images.

name: linkscan
tagline: The broken links, without the false alarms
search: broken link checker no false positives, link checker ignores cloudflare 403, rust site crawler 404 report, linkedin 999 not broken, CI broken link check
summary: Run an ordinary link checker against an ordinary site and the report fills with 403s from Cloudflare, 999s from LinkedIn and timeouts from a slow CDN, none of which are broken links. After the second false alarm nobody opens the report again, which is the same as not having one. This separates a link a visitor would find dead from a link a bot was refused.
how: Three outcomes, not one: broken (404, 410, a 5xx a visitor would see), could not verify (refused or timed out), and works but sends your traffic off your domain. Only the first sets a non-zero exit code.
Every unique URL is checked once however many pages point at it, and every one of those pages is remembered, so the report says where to go and fix it.
HEAD first, GET when HEAD is refused - plenty of servers answer 405 to HEAD while serving GET perfectly.

A 404 on a domain's root is never a deleted page: crates.io answers 404 to anything that is not a browser, and the first version duly reported the Rust homepage as linking to a dead site. Both rules that fixed it are covered by tests.
proof: Six pages of rust-lang.org, 220 unique links checked in 10.5 seconds at 24 concurrent requests. 28 tests, none of which touch the internet.

name: invoice-reconciler
tagline: Match a bank statement against open invoices
search: reconcile bank statement with invoices automatically, payment matching script, part payment batch transfer
summary: Matches payments to invoices in five passes - references, part payments, batch transfers, instalments - and reports only what does not add up. The cases that make manual reconciliation slow are the ones it is built around.
how: Detects the date convention of each file rather than assuming one.
Drops a shortfall that a later payment covered, instead of reporting it twice.
Writes the exception list as CSV or JSON for whoever has to chase it.
proof: Standard library only: it runs on any Python 3.10+ with nothing installed.

name: whatsapp-crm-connector
tagline: WhatsApp Business Cloud webhooks into a CRM
search: WhatsApp Cloud API webhook to CRM, verify X-Hub-Signature-256, 24 hour window token refresh
summary: The parts of a WhatsApp integration that are not the happy path: signature verification, an instant acknowledgement with the work moved to a queue, de-duplication of repeated deliveries, conversations logged against both the contact and the company, the 24-hour window, and token refresh.
how: Verifies the Meta signature over the raw body, and rejects a forged one.
Answers within milliseconds and processes afterwards, because Meta retries anything slow.
Runs offline with one command, against recorded payloads.
proof: 42 tests, including a forged signature that must be refused.

name: email-deliverability-check
tagline: Find out why a domain's mail lands in spam
search: why emails go to spam, SPF too many lookups, DMARC p=none, DKIM revoked, MTA-STS missing
summary: Checks the things that actually put mail in the spam folder: the SPF ten-lookup limit, duplicated records, DKIM keys that have been revoked, DMARC stuck at p=none, and a missing MTA-STS policy. DNS only - no access to the mailbox is needed, which makes it usable on a prospect's domain.
how: Resolves and counts SPF lookups the way a receiving server does.
Batch mode for a list of client domains, with CSV output.
proof: 17 offline checks over recorded DNS answers.

name: repo-secret-scanner
tagline: Catch the key before the push, in one file
search: pre-commit secret scanner no dependencies, find api keys before commit, python leaked token scanner CI, aws key committed by accident, redacted secret report
summary: A key in a commit is public the moment it is pushed and stays in the history after it is deleted, so the only cheap moment to catch it is before the push. The scanners that do this well want an install, a config file and a service account; this is one Python file with no dependencies that exits non-zero on a hit, which is all a pre-commit hook or a CI step needs.
how: Nine rules for the shapes that actually leak: AWS access keys, GitHub, Slack and Google tokens, Stripe live keys, OpenAI-style keys, PEM private-key blocks, JWTs, and bare api_key or password assignments.
Findings are always redacted to first and last four characters plus a length - a report that prints the secret in a CI log has moved the leak rather than stopped it.
--selftest plants a dummy secret and confirms it is caught, so a broken scanner cannot sit there quietly reporting clean.
--entropy is opt-in, because flagging every long string is how a gate gets switched off.
proof: One file, 167 lines, no dependencies; selftest passes on a planted secret. It is the gate I run over my own repositories before every push.
